notes.meaning: The people returning home are called children of the province because Judah was no longer an independent kingdom. It had become a small, subject district under the Persian Empire. The returning exiles went back to their family towns, resettling the places their ancestors had lived before the exile to Babylon.

Zerubbabel, the royal leader from David's line, and Jeshua the high priest led the exiles back to Judah. A group of leaders is named with them, representing the whole nation of Israel rather than just a broken fragment. The Nehemiah and Mordecai listed here are leaders of this early return, not the famous men of the same names found later in the Bible.

The count of returning families begins with the line of Parosh, numbering 2,172 men. The word descendants or children in these verses refers to the male heads of households who traced their line back to this ancestor. God honoured these families by preserving their names in His written record for their faith and courage in returning.

The family of Shephatiah numbered 372 men who made the journey back to their homeland. This exact count matches the later record preserved in Nehemiah. It shows how carefully the leaders kept track of each returning household.

The family of Arah numbered 775 men on this list. A later list in Nehemiah gives a smaller number of 652, which likely means that some who signed up in Babylon grew sick, died, or dropped out before reaching Jerusalem. God still recorded those who originally stepped forward in faith.

The descendants of Pahath-moab formed the largest single clan in this part of the register, totalling 2,812 men. This large clan traced its heritage through two branches, the lines of Jeshua and Joab. Their great size shows how God multiplied this family even while they lived in exile.

The family line of Elam numbered 1,254 men who joined the journey home. This Elam is an ancestral head of a Jewish family, not the foreign land of the same name. Another group with this exact same family name and count appears later in the list.

These verses record the sizes of three more large family clans: Zattu with 945 men, Zaccai with 760, and Bani with 642. Each household head is recognized by name as part of the covenant community returning to Jerusalem. Slight differences between these figures and later registers reflect normal changes during travel or copying.

The descendants of Bebai counted 623 men, and the family of Azgad numbered 1,222. These clans were prominent groups whose relatives would also return in later waves with Ezra. Listing them assured their rightful place and inheritance in the restored community.

The household of Adonikam sent 666 men back from Babylon. While readers sometimes notice the number itself, in this context it is simply the census count of a real Jewish family. They were among the willing remnant that packed up their lives to rebuild God's temple.

Bigvai's clan was one of the largest, sending 2,056 men, while Adin's family numbered 454. Both large and moderate clans were valued equally as part of God's people. Their willingness to return showed their shared love for the land of promise.

The family of Ater, traced through Hezekiah, had 98 men return. This was the smallest clan counted among the ancestral families in this section. Even the smallest families received an honorable place in the sacred register.

Three more family groups are listed here: Bezai with 323 men, Jorah with 112, and Hashum with 223. Each family possessed documented proof of their Hebrew ancestry. God preserved these lineages through seventy years of exile so they could resettle their heritage.

The 95 descendants of Gibbar mark the shift in the chapter from family names to town names. Gibbar is another form of Gibeon, an ancient town in the tribal land of Benjamin. From this point forward, the list identifies people by the ancestral places they came back to inhabit.

Only 123 men returned to Bethlehem, the ancient home of King David. This small number highlights how severely the land had been emptied by war and captivity. Yet this humble town remained precious in God's plan as the promised birthplace of the Messiah.

Netophah was a small village located near Bethlehem, and only 56 of its former residents returned. Although few in number, these villagers took on the hard work of repopulating rural Judah. God remembers even the smallest communities who serve His purposes.

Anathoth was a town of priests where the prophet Jeremiah had lived. Jeremiah had once warned its people of divine judgment, which left the town ruined after the Babylonian invasion. It was a sign of God's mercy that 128 repentant men returned to rebuild this once-smitten city.
